title: Visible light and pigmentation: a 2026 review on why iron-oxide (tinted) sun protection matters for melasma and PIH
headline: A narrative review argues that blue-violet visible light (400 to 450 nm) activates a pigment-cell receptor and drives lasting darkening, and that iron-oxide sunscreens add benefit in melasma; the numbers come from earlier trials I have not opened.
evidenceTier: Narrative review, abstract read; full text paywalled and not opened
fit: Pigment-prone skin: Strong on sun-season fit. The review's main practical point is that UV-only sunscreen leaves visible light unblocked; shade matching is a stated barrier for deeper skin tones.
displaces: It would replace a non-tinted daily sunscreen step or top up pigment-prone zones; it should not add a step.
regions: Global (cosmetic or OTC sunscreen; regulatory status differs by country)
Buy anywhere tinted sunscreens are sold
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
buzzCheck: Sunscreens range widely in price; I did not check prices this run, so I cannot say whether price tracks evidence.
summaryPoints: Abstract (read): high-energy visible light (400 to 450 nm) activates opsin-3 on melanocytes, triggers calcium signalling and raises melanin production in a wavelength-specific way; blue-violet light induced dose-dependent pigment that can persist, red light none.

Reported from earlier work (not opened): melasma patients using iron-oxide sunscreen improved 15% more on MASI, 28% more on colorimetry and 4% more on histology than with a UV-only sunscreen; a suction-blister PIH model healed without darkening at sites shielded from light.

Adherence gap: fewer than two thirds of people with hyperpigmentation use sunscreen and fewer than 10% reapply properly, worse in skin of colour; tint shade mismatch is named as a barrier to using visible-light protection.
Limits: narrative review; the primary trials and their skin-tone mix were not opened by me; the abstract does not say how many studies were pooled.
toneData: Review of mixed literature; authors call for more skin-of-colour data
fitLine: The practical lever with the best fit to melasma and PIH; the open question is a tint that matches deep skin.
timeline: Sunscreen effects build over months in the cited melasma work (not opened)

fitAxes.why: Daily sun protection is a standard companion to a retinoid; not addressed specifically.
Tinted formulations vary in finish and ingredients; not addressed.
Directly about light exposure and pigment.
